warmup.q: In Kotlin, payments.filter { it.settled }.map { it.amountCents } runs on a List. How many lambda objects does one call create?
options: None: filter and map are inline, so the lambda bodies are copied into plain loops
warmup.why: filter and map on Iterable are inline functions. The compiler pastes their loops, and the bodies of your lambdas, into the calling method, so no lambda object is ever created. The call still builds two new ArrayLists, one per step: that is the real cost of a chain, and the next lessons deal with it. Lesson 2's answer, one object per capturing lambda, applies to functions that are not inline.

sections.h: Pass the part that changes in as a function
sections.html:
Look at three places in a payment service that call something flaky:

Java
// authorize
for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    try { auth = issuer.authorize(payment); break; }
    catch (IssuerTimeoutException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; }
}
// post to the ledger: the same loop around ledger.post(entry)
// fetch the FX rate: the same loop around fx.rate("EURUSD")
Kotlin
// authorize
var attempt = 1
while (true) {
    try { auth = issuer.authorize(payment); break }
    catch (e: IssuerTimeoutException) { if (attempt++ == 3) throw e }
}
// post to the ledger: the same loop around ledger.post(entry)
// fetch the FX rate: the same loop around fx.rate("EURUSD")

The three loops are identical except for one call. An ordinary helper method can't pull that call out, because a method's parameters are values, and the call has to happen inside the loop, up to three times. What you need to pass in is the work itself.

A higher-order function is a function that takes a function as a parameter, returns one, or both. Here is retry written as one:

Java
static <T> T retry(int times, Supplier<T> block) {
    RuntimeException last = null;
    for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= times; attempt++) {
        try { return block.get(); }
        catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; }
    }
    throw new IllegalStateException("gave up after " + times + " attempts", last);
}

String auth = retry(3, () -> issuer.authorize(payment));
Kotlin
fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: () -> T): T {
    var last: Exception? = null
    repeat(times) {
        try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { last = e }
    }
    throw IllegalStateException("gave up after $times attempts", last)
}

val auth = retry(3) { issuer.authorize(payment) }

The loop is written once. The part that varies, the call, arrives as block, and retry decides when and how often to run it. That is the whole idea of this lesson: keep the shape of a computation (retry it, time it, cache it) apart from the work inside it. (The return inside repeat leaves retry itself. That only works because repeat is inline, which the last section explains.)

Kotlin makes the call site read like a language feature. When the last parameter is a function, you can write the lambda after the parentheses, a trailing lambda, and if it's the only argument you drop the parentheses too: retry(3) { ... }, timed("auth") { ... }. That's why repeat, synchronized, use and buildList look built in. They are ordinary library functions.

Java needs an interface for the parameter, and checked exceptions get in the way. Supplier.get() can't throw an IOException, so retrying I/O needs a Callable<T> and a throws Exception on retry. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so () -> T fits every call.

try.title: One retry loop for every flaky call
steps: Run Retry (or RetryJava). Predict first: how many calls reach the issuer in each half?
Wrap the second retry in timed("gave up") { ... } as well. Predict whether its timing line prints, even though the block throws.
Change the first retry(3) to retry(1) and run again.

code.title: Retry.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo // A fake card issuer that times out a few times, then answers. class FlakyIssuer(private var failuresLeft: Int) { var calls = 0 fun authorize(paymentId: String): String { calls++ if (failuresLeft-- > 0) throw IllegalStateException("issuer timeout on call $calls") return "auth_$paymentId" } } // A higher-order function: the loop is written once, and the work comes in as a function. fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: () -> T): T { var last: Exception? = null repeat(times) { attempt -> try { return block() // returns from retry: repeat is inline } catch (e: Exception) { last = e println(" attempt ${attempt + 1} failed: ${e.message}") } } throw IllegalStateException("gave up after $times attempts", last) } // Another one: run any block, report how long it took, hand back its result unchanged. fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println(" $label took %.2f ms".format((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e6)) } } fun main() { val issuer = FlakyIssuer(failuresLeft = 2) val auth = timed("authorize with retry") { retry(3) { issuer.authorize("pay_42") } } println("result: $auth after ${issuer.calls} calls") val down = FlakyIssuer(failuresLeft = 5) try { retry(3) { down.authorize("pay_43") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("result: ${e.message} (last cause: ${e.cause?.message})") } }

alt.title: RetryJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** * Java twin of Retry.kt. The work comes in as a Supplier<T>. Supplier.get() can't throw checked * exceptions, so code that throws IOException needs Callable<T> and a `throws Exception` on retry. */ public class RetryJava { static final class FlakyIssuer { private int failuresLeft; int calls = 0; FlakyIssuer(int failuresLeft) { this.failuresLeft = failuresLeft; } String authorize(String paymentId) { calls++; if (failuresLeft-- > 0) throw new IllegalStateException("issuer timeout on call " + calls); return "auth_" + paymentId; } } // A higher-order method: the loop is written once, and the work comes in as a function. static <T> T retry(int times, Supplier<T> block) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= times; attempt++) { try { return block.get(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; System.out.println(" attempt " + attempt + " failed: " + e.getMessage()); } } throw new IllegalStateException("gave up after " + times + " attempts", last); } // Another one: run any block, report how long it took, hand back its result unchanged. static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.printf(" %s took %.2f ms%n", label, (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e6); } } public static void main(String[] args) { FlakyIssuer issuer = new FlakyIssuer(2); String auth = timed("authorize with retry", () -> retry(3, () -> issuer.authorize("pay_42"))); System.out.println("result: " + auth + " after " + issuer.calls + " calls"); FlakyIssuer down = new FlakyIssuer(5); try { retry(3, () -> down.authorize("pay_43")); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("result: " + e.getMessage() + " (last cause: " + e.getCause().getMessage() + ")"); } } }

try.expect: The first half takes three calls: two timeouts, then auth_pay_42. The second gives up after three: gave up after 3 attempts (last cause: issuer timeout on call 3). timed prints its line even when the block throws, because the print is in a finally. With retry(1), the program stops with IllegalStateException: gave up after 1 attempts. retry never changed in any of these runs; only the function you handed it did.

sections.h: Return a function: build the fee rule once
sections.html:
Higher-order works in the other direction too. A function can build another function and hand it back.

Java
static Function<Long, Long> feeFor(String country) {
    long bps = RATES_BPS.get(country);                   // looked up once
    return amountCents -> amountCents * bps / 10_000;
}

Function<Long, Long> dutch = feeFor("NL");
dutch.apply(100_000L);                                   // 1400
Kotlin
fun feeFor(country: String): (Long) -> Long {
    val bps = RATES_BPS.getValue(country)                // looked up once
    return { amountCents -> amountCents * bps / 10_000 }
}

val dutch = feeFor("NL")
dutch(100_000)                                           // 1400

fee(country, amount) needs two arguments. feeFor(country) takes the first one now and gives back a function that waits for the second. Fixing some of a function's arguments and getting back a function of the rest is called partial application.

It pays off when the first argument is known early and the second arrives many times. A settlement job knows each merchant's country at startup and then computes thousands of fees. feeFor looks the rate up once, and the closure it returns (lesson 2) keeps only the number it needs. It also moves failure to the right moment. An unknown country fails when you build the function, at startup, not on the first payment at 3 a.m.

Currying takes the same idea all the way: every function takes exactly one argument and returns a function for the next. A curried fee has the type (String) -> (Long) -> Long. The arrows group to the right, so read it as (String) -> ((Long) -> Long).

Java
Function<String, Function<Long, Long>> curriedFee = country -> amount -> fee(country, amount);
curriedFee.apply("DE").apply(100_000L);                  // 1500
Kotlin
val curriedFee: (String) -> (Long) -> Long = { country -> { amount -> fee(country, amount) } }
curriedFee("DE")(100_000)                                // 1500

Haskell curries every function. In Kotlin, don't. The signatures get hard to read, the IDE hints get noisy, and Kotlin already covers what currying is for: a lambda that fixes one argument ({ a: Long -> fee("US", a) }), default and named arguments, and bound references like merchant::fee. Write a function that returns a function when you mean "configure now, run many times", like feeFor. That's the case that earns its keep.

try.title: When does a bad country fail?
steps: Run FeeFor (or FeeForJava) and check one number: 140 basis points of 100,000 cents is 1,400.
Add val broken = feeFor("XX") as the first line of main, without calling broken. Predict whether the program fails, and where.

Move the lookup into the returned lambda: return { amountCents -> amountCents * RATES_BPS.getValue(country) / 10_000 } (Java: RATES_BPS.get(country) inside the lambda). Run again. Now when does it fail?

code.title: FeeFor.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo val RATES_BPS = mapOf("NL" to 140L, "DE" to 150L, "US" to 290L) // basis points: 1 bp = 0.01 % // Both arguments at once. fun fee(country: String, amountCents: Long): Long = amountCents * RATES_BPS.getValue(country) / 10_000 // Partial application: fix the country now, get back a function of the amount. fun feeFor(country: String): (Long) -> Long { val bps = RATES_BPS.getValue(country) // looked up once, right here return { amountCents -> amountCents * bps / 10_000 } } // Currying by hand: take one argument, return a function that takes the next one. val curriedFee: (String) -> (Long) -> Long = { country -> { amountCents -> fee(country, amountCents) } } fun main() { val dutch = feeFor("NL") println("feeFor(\"NL\")(100000) = ${dutch(100_000)}") println("curriedFee(\"DE\")(100000) = ${curriedFee("DE")(100_000)}") // Kotlin idioms that usually read better than a curried signature: val usFee = { amountCents: Long -> fee("US", amountCents) } // a lambda that fixes one argument println("lambda that fixes US = ${usFee(100_000)}") println("named arguments = ${fee(amountCents = 100_000, country = "NL")}") val amounts = listOf(10_000L, 250_000L, 1_000_000L) println("amounts.map(dutch) = ${amounts.map(dutch)}") }

alt.title: FeeForJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of FeeFor.kt. Partial application and currying with java.util.function.Function. */ public class FeeForJava { static final Map<String, Long> RATES_BPS = Map.of("NL", 140L, "DE", 150L, "US", 290L); // Both arguments at once. static long fee(String country, long amountCents) { return amountCents * RATES_BPS.get(country) / 10_000; } // Partial application: fix the country now, get back a function of the amount. static Function<Long, Long> feeFor(String country) { long bps = RATES_BPS.get(country); // looked up once, right here return amountCents -> amountCents * bps / 10_000; } // Currying by hand: the type says it all. static final Function<String, Function<Long, Long>> CURRIED_FEE = country -> amountCents -> fee(country, amountCents); public static void main(String[] args) { Function<Long, Long> dutch = feeFor("NL"); System.out.println("feeFor(\"NL\").apply(100000) = " + dutch.apply(100_000L)); System.out.println("CURRIED_FEE.apply(\"DE\").apply(100000) = " + CURRIED_FEE.apply("DE").apply(100_000L)); // A lambda that fixes one argument. (Java has no named arguments.) Function<Long, Long> usFee = amountCents -> fee("US", amountCents); System.out.println("lambda that fixes US = " + usFee.apply(100_000L)); List<Long> amounts = List.of(10_000L, 250_000L, 1_000_000L); System.out.println("amounts.stream().map(dutch) = " + amounts.stream().map(dutch).toList()); } }

try.expect: With the lookup outside the lambda, feeFor("XX") fails right away: Kotlin throws NoSuchElementException: Key XX is missing in the map., and Java throws a NullPointerException when it unboxes the missing rate. With the lookup inside the lambda, feeFor("XX") succeeds and returns a function that fails on its first call, which could be hours later in production. Same code, different moment of failure. You want the first one.

sections.h: Compose small functions into a pipeline
sections.html:
Fee adjustments come in small pieces: add a 25-cent scheme fee, take 10 % off for loyal merchants, cap at 10 euros. Each piece is a (Long) -> Long. A merchant's price is some of those pieces run one after another, and each merchant has a different set.

Running one function on the result of another is called composition. Java's Function interface has it built in, as two default methods, andThen and compose:

Java
Function<Long, Long> price = addSchemeFee.andThen(loyaltyDiscount).andThen(capAtTenEuros);
price.apply(1_200L);                                      // 1000
Kotlin
infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) }

val price = addSchemeFee andThen loyaltyDiscount andThen capAtTenEuros
price(1_200)                                              // 1000

Kotlin's standard library has no andThen or compose for function types. Without the one-line extension above, addSchemeFee andThen loyaltyDiscount fails with unresolved reference 'andThen' on receiver of type '(Long) -> Long'. Arrow, the best-known functional library for Kotlin, ships andThen, compose and curried in a separate arrow-functions module. This track's lab doesn't depend on it. One line is all you need, and writing it shows there is no magic: this is the first function, this(a) calls it, and next gets the result. infix lets you write it without dots and parentheses, so the steps read left to right in the order they run. compose is the same with the arguments swapped, (g compose f)(x) == g(f(x)), as mathematicians write it. Pick one and stay with it. andThen matches the way people read.

Two things about composition matter in practice. The order is part of the result: capping before the scheme fee gives 922 cents, capping after it gives 1,000. And a list of steps folds into one function, starting from the function that returns its input unchanged:

Java
Function<Long, Long> merchantPrice = steps.stream()
        .reduce(Function.identity(), (acc, step) -> acc.andThen(step));
Kotlin
val merchantPrice = steps.fold({ x: Long -> x }) { acc, step -> acc andThen step }

That's how configuration becomes code. Read a merchant's adjustments at startup, turn each row into a function, fold them into one (Long) -> Long, and call it for every payment. Every piece stays small, pure and testable on its own. (Lesson 4 covers fold properly.)

try.title: Compose, reorder, extend
steps: Run Compose (or ComposeJava). Predict both prices for 500 and for 1,200 before you look.
Delete the andThen extension at the top of Compose.kt and run again. Read the error, then put the line back.
Add a fourth step, val roundToTen: (Long) -> Long = { it / 10 * 10 }, at the end of steps, and print fromList(900). Predict it first.

code.title: Compose.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo // The stdlib has no andThen for function types, so here it is. Remove it and the file stops compiling. infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) } val addSchemeFee: (Long) -> Long = { it + 25 } // +25 cents val loyaltyDiscount: (Long) -> Long = { it * 90 / 100 } // 10 % off, rounded down val capAtTenEuros: (Long) -> Long = { minOf(it, 1_000) } fun main() { val price = addSchemeFee andThen loyaltyDiscount andThen capAtTenEuros val capFirst = capAtTenEuros andThen addSchemeFee andThen loyaltyDiscount for (fee in listOf(500L, 1_200L)) { println("fee $fee -> ${price(fee)} (cap first: ${capFirst(fee)})") } // Built from a list, the way merchant configuration would build it. val steps = listOf(addSchemeFee, loyaltyDiscount, capAtTenEuros) val fromList = steps.fold({ x: Long -> x }) { acc, step -> acc andThen step } println("fromList(1200) = ${fromList(1_200)}") }

alt.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of Compose.kt. java.util.function.Function has andThen and compose built in, as default methods. */ public class ComposeJava { static final Function<Long, Long> ADD_SCHEME_FEE = fee -> fee + 25; // +25 cents static final Function<Long, Long> LOYALTY_DISCOUNT = fee -> fee * 90 / 100; // 10 % off, rounded down static final Function<Long, Long> CAP_AT_TEN_EUROS = fee -> Math.min(fee, 1_000); public static void main(String[] args) { Function<Long, Long> price = ADD_SCHEME_FEE.andThen(LOYALTY_DISCOUNT).andThen(CAP_AT_TEN_EUROS); Function<Long, Long> capFirst = CAP_AT_TEN_EUROS.andThen(ADD_SCHEME_FEE).andThen(LOYALTY_DISCOUNT); for (long fee : new long[] {500L, 1_200L}) { System.out.println("fee " + fee + " -> " + price.apply(fee) + " (cap first: " + capFirst.apply(fee) + ")"); } // Built from a list, the way merchant configuration would build it. List<Function<Long, Long>> steps = List.of(ADD_SCHEME_FEE, LOYALTY_DISCOUNT, CAP_AT_TEN_EUROS); Function<Long, Long> fromList = steps.stream() .reduce(Function.identity(), (acc, step) -> acc.andThen(step)); System.out.println("fromList(1200) = " + fromList.apply(1_200L)); } }

try.expect: 500 gives 472 both ways, because the cap never bites. 1,200 gives 1,000 with the cap last and 922 with the cap first. Without the extension, Kotlin reports unresolved reference 'andThen' on receiver of type '(Long) -> Long'. The Java version has nothing to delete: andThen is a default method on Function. With roundToTen, fromList(900) goes 925, then 832, then 832 again (under the cap), then 830.

sections.h: memoize: a function that remembers its answers
sections.html:
A higher-order function can also take a function and return an improved version of it. memoize returns a function that gives the same answers as the original but computes each one only once.

Java
static <A, R> Function<A, R> memoize(Function<A, R> f) {
    Map<A, R> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    return a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a, f);
}

Function<String, String> country = memoize(Bins::issuerCountry);
Kotlin
fun <A : Any, R : Any> memoize(f: (A) -> R): (A) -> R {
    val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<A, R>()
    return { a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a) { f(it) } }
}

val country = memoize(::issuerCountry)

Everything from the last lesson is in those four lines. memoize takes a function and returns one. The returned lambda is a closure over cache, so each memoized function gets its own map that nobody else can reach. It's safe on many threads because the captured state is a ConcurrentHashMap held in a val, not a var. computeIfAbsent runs f at most once per key, even when two threads ask for the same key at the same moment, as the concurrent collections lesson showed. The A : Any, R : Any bounds are there because ConcurrentHashMap can't store null.

Memoizing is only correct for pure functions. Referential transparency, from lesson 1, says a pure call can be replaced by its value, and a cache does exactly that replacement for you. Memoize something impure and you get stale answers. In the demo, a memoized FX rate keeps returning 1.08 after the market moves to 1.11, and it will keep doing so until the process restarts. Mapping a card BIN to its issuer country from a fixed table is a good fit. Today's exchange rate, an account balance or anything you read from a database is not.

Two practical limits. The cache never forgets, so only memoize over a small, known set of keys (countries, currencies, BIN prefixes), never over payment ids. When you need expiry or a size limit, use a real cache library such as Caffeine, which is the same idea plus eviction. And the function you pass to computeIfAbsent must not change the same map, so this memoize can't wrap a recursive function that calls its own memoized version.

try.title: A cache that helps, and one that lies
steps: Run Memoize (or MemoizeJava). Predict the number of lookups for the five BINs, and roughly how long they take (each real lookup sleeps 50 ms).
Replace memoize(::issuerCountry) with plain ::issuerCountry and run again.
Explain the last line of the output to yourself before you read the expected result. Why is the memoized rate wrong?

code.title: Memoize.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap // A higher-order function that returns a function: same answers as f, but each one computed once. fun <A : Any, R : Any> memoize(f: (A) -> R): (A) -> R { val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<A, R>() // captured: one cache per memoized function return { a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a) { f(it) } } } // Pure but slow: imagine it scans a large BIN table on every call. var binLookups = 0 fun issuerCountry(bin: String): String { binLookups++ Thread.sleep(50) return if (bin.startsWith("4")) "NL" else "DE" } // Impure: the exchange rate moves while the service runs. var eurUsd = 1.08 fun fxRate(pair: String): Double = if (pair == "EURUSD") eurUsd else 1.0 fun main() { val country = memoize(::issuerCountry) val bins = listOf("424242", "555555", "424242", "424242", "555555") val start = System.nanoTime() println(bins.map(country)) println("lookups: $binLookups for ${bins.size} calls, %d ms".format((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000)) val rate = memoize(::fxRate) println("EURUSD now: ${rate("EURUSD")}") eurUsd = 1.11 // the market moves println("EURUSD after the market moved: ${rate("EURUSD")} (real rate: ${fxRate("EURUSD")})") }

alt.title: MemoizeJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of Memoize.kt. */ public class MemoizeJava { // A higher-order method that returns a function: same answers as f, but each one computed once. static <A, R> Function<A, R> memoize(Function<A, R> f) { Map<A, R> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // captured: one cache per memoized function return a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a, f); } // Pure but slow: imagine it scans a large BIN table on every call. static int binLookups = 0; static String issuerCountry(String bin) { binLookups++; try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return bin.startsWith("4") ? "NL" : "DE"; } // Impure: the exchange rate moves while the service runs. static double eurUsd = 1.08; static double fxRate(String pair) { return pair.equals("EURUSD") ? eurUsd : 1.0; } public static void main(String[] args) { Function<String, String> country = memoize(MemoizeJava::issuerCountry); List<String> bins = List.of("424242", "555555", "424242", "424242", "555555"); long start = System.nanoTime(); System.out.println(bins.stream().map(country).toList()); System.out.printf("lookups: %d for %d calls, %d ms%n", binLookups, bins.size(), (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000); Function<String, Double> rate = memoize(MemoizeJava::fxRate); System.out.println("EURUSD now: " + rate.apply("EURUSD")); eurUsd = 1.11; // the market moves System.out.println("EURUSD after the market moved: " + rate.apply("EURUSD") + " (real rate: " + fxRate("EURUSD") + ")"); } }

try.expect: Memoized: 2 lookups for 5 calls, a little over 100 ms. Without memoize: 5 lookups, about 250 ms, and the same answers. The FX line prints 1.08 after the rate moved to 1.11. fxRate reads a mutable global, so it is impure, and the cache froze its first answer. A cache is only invisible when the function it wraps is pure.

sections.h: inline: why map and filter cost no lambdas
sections.html:
Every lambda you pass to retry or memoize is an object (lesson 2), and a var it changes becomes a Ref box. So you might expect payments.filter { ... }.map { ... } to create two lambda objects on every call. It creates none, because filter, map, forEach, fold, sumOf and almost every other collection function on Iterable are declared inline.

When you call an inline function, the compiler doesn't emit a call. It copies the function's body into the call site, and the lambda's body with it. The lambda never exists as an object.

Java
// Java has no inline functions. The method reference is a lambda object
// (shared, since it captures nothing), and only the JIT may inline it at runtime.
long total = payments.stream().mapToLong(Payment::amountCents).sum();
Kotlin
inline fun <T> measuredInline(block: () -> T): T {
    val start = System.nanoTime()
    val result = block()
    lastNanos = System.nanoTime() - start
    return result
}

var total = 0L
measuredInline { amounts.forEach { total += it } }   // becomes a plain loop; total stays a local

The demo compiles two versions of the same code. With a non-inline measured, the bytecode has new Ref$LongRef for total, an invokedynamic for the lambda and a call through Function0.invoke. With measuredInline it has none of them: the System.nanoTime() calls, the iterator loop and an ladd on a local variable are pasted straight into totalInlined. That is also why return inside repeat worked in retry. After inlining, the lambda body is part of retry, so return leaves retry. This is called a non-local return, and it's only allowed when the lambda is inlined.

So mark your own small higher-order functions inline when they take a lambda and call it straight away, as measuredInline and retry do. Don't mark everything inline. The body is copied into every call site, so a big inline function bloats the code. And a lambda you keep for later, like the f that memoize stores in its closure, can't be inlined: the compiler needs a real object to keep. The Advanced Kotlin track, later in this part of the course, has a whole lesson on inline, noinline, crossinline and non-local returns.

try.title: Find the missing lambda in the bytecode
steps: Run InlineCost. Both totals print 13400. (Java has no inline functions, so this demo has no Java twin.)

From labs/, run javap -c -p functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/functional/l03/demo/InlineCostKt.class. Compare totalWithLambda with totalInlined: look for Ref$LongRef, invokedynamic and System.nanoTime.
Predict what changes in totalInlined if you delete the word inline from measuredInline. Then try it.

code.title: InlineCost.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo var lastNanos = 0L // Not inline: the lambda becomes an object, and a var it changes becomes a Ref box. fun <T> measured(block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() val result = block() lastNanos = System.nanoTime() - start return result } // Inline: the compiler pastes this body, and the lambda's body, into every caller. inline fun <T> measuredInline(block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() val result = block() lastNanos = System.nanoTime() - start return result } fun totalWithLambda(amounts: List<Long>): Long { var total = 0L measured { for (a in amounts) total += a } return total } fun totalInlined(amounts: List<Long>): Long { var total = 0L measuredInline { amounts.forEach { total += it } } return total } fun main() { val amounts = listOf(1_500L, 9_900L, 2_000L) println("with a lambda object: ${totalWithLambda(amounts)}") println("inlined: ${totalInlined(amounts)}") }

try.expect: totalWithLambda has new kotlin/jvm/internal/Ref$LongRef, an invokedynamic that makes a Function0, and a call to measured. totalInlined has none of them: it calls System.nanoTime itself and adds into a local with ladd. Without inline, totalInlined looks like totalWithLambda: a Ref$LongRef, an invokedynamic and a call to measuredInline. measuredInline also exists as an ordinary method in the class, for callers such as Java code that can't inline it.

analogy: A higher-order function is a standard procedure with a blank in it. "Call the system; if it times out, try again, up to three times" works for the issuer, the ledger and the FX service, and you fill in which call. Partial application is a pre-filled form: the country is already written in, so the clerk only adds the amount. Composition is an assembly line where each station does one small job and passes the part on, and moving a station changes the product. The analogy breaks at memoize: a paper procedure doesn't remember what happened last time, and that memory is exactly why memoize only suits answers that never change.
world: Your Quarkus services already wrap calls in retry and timing logic, mostly through annotations: MicroProfile Fault Tolerance's @Retry and @Timeout, Micrometer's @Timed. Those are higher-order functions in disguise: the framework takes your method and returns a wrapped one. A hand-written retry(3) { issuer.authorize(p) } fits where annotations can't reach, such as one call inside a Kafka consumer loop. Partial application fits per-merchant configuration: when a merchant's config loads, build its (Long) -> Long fee function once and keep it in a map. In Temporal, leave activity retries to the activity's RetryOptions rather than a loop of your own, so the server tracks attempts and backoff for you.
mistake: The most common mistake is memoizing a function that isn't pure. It's tempting to wrap an exchange-rate lookup, a merchant-config read or an account lookup in memoize to save a database call, and in a test it looks perfect. In production the cache keeps its first answer forever: the rate moves, the config changes, and the memoized function never notices. A quieter version is memoizing over keys that never repeat, such as payment ids, which turns the cache into a memory leak. Memoize only pure functions over a small, known set of keys. For data that changes, use a real cache with expiry (Caffeine, or your framework's cache) and decide how stale an answer you can accept.

compare.title: Functions in, functions out, functions combined

java.title: Fees.java
java.html: import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.function.Function; import java.util.function.Supplier; final class Fees { // functions in static <T> T retry(int times, Supplier<T> block) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) { try { return block.get(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; } } throw new IllegalStateException("gave up after " + times + " attempts", last); } // functions out: partial application static Function<Long, Long> feeFor(long bps) { return amountCents -> amountCents * bps / 10_000; } // composition is built into Function static Function<Long, Long> price(long bps) { return feeFor(bps).andThen(fee -> fee + 25).andThen(fee -> Math.min(fee, 1_000)); } static <A, R> Function<A, R> memoize(Function<A, R> f) { Map<A, R> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); return a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a, f); } }

kotlin.title: Fees.kt
kotlin.html: import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap // functions in; inline, so the lambda is pasted into the caller inline fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: () -> T): T { var last: Exception? = null repeat(times) { try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { last = e } } throw IllegalStateException("gave up after $times attempts", last) } // functions out: partial application fun feeFor(bps: Long): (Long) -> Long = { amountCents -> amountCents * bps / 10_000 } // composition is not in the stdlib: one line of your own infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) } fun price(bps: Long): (Long) -> Long = feeFor(bps) andThen { fee -> fee + 25 } andThen { fee -> minOf(fee, 1_000) } fun <A : Any, R : Any> memoize(f: (A) -> R): (A) -> R { val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<A, R>() return { a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a) { f(it) } } }

compare.note: Both languages make the same three moves: functions in, functions out, functions combined. The differences are in the plumbing. Java's Function comes with andThen and compose, and Kotlin's function types don't, so you write the extension yourself or use Arrow's arrow-functions module. Java needs a different interface per shape (Supplier, Function, Callable once checked exceptions appear), while Kotlin uses () -> T and (A) -> R everywhere. And Kotlin can declare a higher-order function inline, so the lambda passed to retry is pasted into the caller and never allocated. Java leaves that to the JIT, which may or may not inline at runtime.

worked.title: Turn a merchant's fee configuration into one function

steps.say: A merchant's fee configuration is a list of rows loaded at startup: a kind of adjustment and a number. We want one (Long) -> Long per merchant, built once, called for every payment.
steps.code: data class AdjustmentRow(val kind: String, val value: Long) val acmeRows = listOf( AdjustmentRow("discount", 10), // 10 % off AdjustmentRow("floor", 50), // at least 50 cents AdjustmentRow("cap", 1_000), // at most 10 euros )

alt.html: record AdjustmentRow(String kind, long value) {} List<AdjustmentRow> acmeRows = List.of( new AdjustmentRow("discount", 10), // 10 % off new AdjustmentRow("floor", 50), // at least 50 cents new AdjustmentRow("cap", 1_000)); // at most 10 euros

steps.say: 1. Turn each row into a function with a when expression. Each branch returns a function, and nothing is computed yet. An unknown kind is a configuration bug, so it throws here.
steps.code: fun toAdjust(row: AdjustmentRow): (Long) -> Long = when (row.kind) { "flat" -> { fee -> fee + row.value } "discount" -> { fee -> fee * (100 - row.value) / 100 } "floor" -> { fee -> maxOf(fee, row.value) } "cap" -> { fee -> minOf(fee, row.value) } else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown adjustment ${row.kind}") }

alt.html: static Function<Long, Long> toAdjust(AdjustmentRow row) { return switch (row.kind()) { case "flat" -> fee -> fee + row.value(); case "discount" -> fee -> fee * (100 - row.value()) / 100; case "floor" -> fee -> Math.max(fee, row.value()); case "cap" -> fee -> Math.min(fee, row.value()); default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown adjustment " + row.kind()); }; }

steps.say: 1. Fold the adjustments onto the country's base fee. Self-check: when does a row with an unknown kind fail, at startup or on the first payment? (At startup: toAdjust runs inside map, while the function is being built.)
steps.code: fun merchantFee(country: String, rows: List<AdjustmentRow>): (Long) -> Long = rows.map(::toAdjust) // 1. rows to functions .fold(feeFor(country)) { acc, f -> acc andThen f } // 2. one function, base fee first

alt.html: static Function<Long, Long> merchantFee(String country, List<AdjustmentRow> rows) { return rows.stream() .map(Fees::toAdjust) // 1. rows to functions .reduce(feeFor(country), Function::andThen); // 2. one function, base fee first }

steps.say: 1. Build once per merchant, call per payment. Each payment now costs four small calls and no lookups, and every adjustment can be tested on its own with plain numbers.
steps.code: val acmeFee = merchantFee("NL", acmeRows) acmeFee(100_000) // 1,400 -> 1,260 -> 1,260 -> 1,000 acmeFee(2_000) // 28 -> 25 -> 50 -> 50

alt.html: Function<Long, Long> acmeFee = merchantFee("NL", acmeRows); acmeFee.apply(100_000L); // 1,400 -> 1,260 -> 1,260 -> 1,000 acmeFee.apply(2_000L); // 28 -> 25 -> 50 -> 50

lab.title: Compose a fee pipeline, and memoize a slow lookup
steps: Run the tests. All ten fail with NotImplementedError. Read the four finished building blocks at the top of Pipeline.kt: each one is a function that returns a function.
Write andThen and compose. Each body is one lambda.
Write pipeline with fold, starting from { x: T -> x }. An empty list must give back that identity function.
Write feeFor. Do the rate lookup outside the lambda you return, and throw IllegalArgumentException("no rate for $country") for an unknown country.
Write merchantFee from feeFor, andThen and pipeline. Then write curried.
Write memoize in Memo.kt. Run the tests until all ten pass.
hints: andThen is { a -> next(this(a)) }. Inside an extension on a function type, this is the function, and this(a) calls it.
requireNotNull(BASIS_POINTS[country]) { "no rate for $country" } returns the rate, or throws IllegalArgumentException with that message.

ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent(key) { f(it) } calls f only when the key is missing. A HashMap with getOrPut also passes these tests, but it isn't safe once several threads share the memoized function.

drill.title: Write retry and andThen from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write an inline function retry(times, block) that calls block until it returns, at most times times, and then throws IllegalStateException with the last failure as its cause. Write andThen for function types. Use both: retry a call that returns a fee in cents, then run the fee through { it + 25 } andThen { minOf(it, 1_000) }. Then write the Java version of both functions.

answer.html: inline fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: () -> T): T { var last: Exception? = null repeat(times) { try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { last = e } // non-local return: repeat is inline } throw IllegalStateException("gave up after $times attempts", last) } infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) } val adjust: (Long) -> Long = { fee: Long -> fee + 25 } andThen { fee -> minOf(fee, 1_000) } val fee = adjust(retry(3) { pricing.baseFee(payment) })

alt.html: static <T> T retry(int times, Supplier<T> block) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) { try { return block.get(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; } } throw new IllegalStateException("gave up after " + times + " attempts", last); } // andThen is already a default method on java.util.function.Function Function<Long, Long> addScheme = fee -> fee + 25; Function<Long, Long> adjust = addScheme.andThen(fee -> Math.min(fee, 1_000)); long fee = adjust.apply(retry(3, () -> pricing.baseFee(payment)));

recap: A higher-order function takes a function, returns one, or both. It keeps the shape of a computation (retry, time, cache) apart from the work inside it.
Trailing lambdas make higher-order calls read like built-ins: retry(3) { issuer.authorize(p) }.
Returning a function gives you partial application: feeFor(country) looks up the rate once and returns a (Long) -> Long. Prefer that, or a plain lambda, to curried signatures.
Kotlin's stdlib has no andThen or compose for function types; write the one-line infix extension (Java's Function has both). Order matters, and a list of steps folds into one function.
Memoize only pure functions, over a small set of keys. A memoized impure function returns stale answers until restart.
inline pastes a function and its lambda into the call site: no lambda object, no Ref box, and return leaves the enclosing function. That's why map and filter on lists create no lambdas.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why payments.filter { it.settled }.map { it.amountCents } creates no lambda objects, while their own fun <T> timed(block: () -> T): T does. Explain it in your own words, and say what you'd change in timed.
explain.answer: A lambda is normally an object: a function value that something has to create, and if it changes a captured var, that var moves into a Ref box. filter and map on lists are declared inline, so the compiler never calls them. It copies their loops into my method and pastes my lambda bodies into those loops, and no lambda object ever exists. timed isn't inline, so its block has to be a real object passed to a real call. Since timed only calls block once, right away, I'd mark it inline. Then the timing code and the block are pasted into each caller, with no allocation and no Ref box. I wouldn't do that for a function that stores its lambda, like memoize, because a stored lambda has to be an object.

deeper.html:
Kotlin gives you partial application in a few forms besides returning a lambda. A bound reference fixes the receiver, which is often all you need:

Java
final class Merchant {
    private final long bps;
    Merchant(long bps) { this.bps = bps; }
    long fee(long amountCents) { return amountCents * bps / 10_000; }
}

Merchant acme = new Merchant(140);
Function<Long, Long> acmeFee = acme::fee;          // a bound method reference
List.of(10_000L, 50_000L).stream().map(acmeFee).toList();   // [140, 700]
Kotlin
class Merchant(private val bps: Long) {
    fun fee(amountCents: Long): Long = amountCents * bps / 10_000
}

val acme = Merchant(bps = 140)
val acmeFee: (Long) -> Long = acme::fee          // a bound reference: the receiver is fixed
listOf(10_000L, 50_000L).map(acmeFee)            // [140, 700]

This is the strategy pattern with the ceremony removed: an object with one behaviour, passed around as a function. Remember lesson 2's detail, though: in Kotlin 2.4.21 a bound reference compiles to a small class and allocates one object each time the expression runs.

Arrow 2.3.0 puts its function utilities in the io.arrow-kt:arrow-functions artifact, separate from arrow-core. Its jar contains andThen and compose, curried and uncurried with overloads up to 22 parameters, partially1 and its siblings, and memoize. If your codebase already uses Arrow, use those rather than your own. If it doesn't, the one-line versions in this lesson are not a reason to add a dependency.

One more look at inline and return. Inside an inline higher-order function's lambda, a bare return leaves the enclosing function, and return@forEach (or any label) leaves only the lambda, acting like continue. Java developers moving to Kotlin trip on this in forEach, because a return in a Java Stream.forEach lambda only ends that one call. The Advanced Kotlin track's inline lesson goes through noinline and crossinline, the two modifiers that control which lambdas get pasted and where return may go.
